title: Dual Special Needs Plans (D-SNP) Frequently Asked Questions
summary: Answers common questions about dual eligibility, D-SNP benefits, enrollment periods, costs, losing Medicaid, and how D-SNPs differ from C-SNPs and Medicare-Medicaid Plans.

assets.alt: Hero image for Dual Special Needs plans FAQs

atoms.title: What does dual eligible mean?
atoms.question: What does dual eligible mean?
atoms.text: People who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid at the same time are dual eligible; they are eligible for both health care programs. Some people receive benefits from both programs. They qualify for Medicare because of age (65 or older) or a disability, and they are eligible for Medicaid because they meet their state's requirements.
questions: What does it mean to be dual eligible?
Can you have Medicare and Medicaid at the same time?

atoms.title: Difference between Medicare and Medicaid
atoms.question: What's the difference between Medicare and Medicaid?
atoms.text: Medicare is a national health insurance program run by the federal government for people age 65 and older, and also some people under 65 with certain disabilities. Medicaid is a joint program funded together by states and the federal government. Children, pregnant women, elderly adults and people with disabilities, as well as eligible low-income adults, are typically covered by Medicaid.

Who is covered by Medicaid versus Medicare?

atoms.title: How you qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid
atoms.question: How do you qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid?
atoms.text: They are two separate programs with different eligibility requirements. For Medicare you need to be at least 65, or under 65 and qualify on the basis of disability or other special situations, and be a U.S. citizen or legal resident who has lived in the U.S. for at least 5 years in a row. For state Medicaid you need to be under 65 and meet requirements for low-income families, pregnant women and children, SSI, disability or other special situations, or be 65 or older and also receive Extra Help or state assistance, or be blind or have a disability but not need long-term care.
questions: What do I need to qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid?

atoms.title: How Medicare and Medicaid work together
atoms.question: How do Medicare and Medicaid work together?
atoms.text: Medicaid programs often cover benefits that Medicare doesn't offer, such as dental, vision and hearing coverage, transportation assistance and long-term care. Paying for certain Medicare costs is another way Medicaid can help Medicare. The Medicare-Medicaid Coordination Office, created within CMS as part of the Affordable Care Act, is responsible for making sure dually enrolled people have seamless, high quality health care.

atoms.title: Advantages of a Dual Special Needs plan
atoms.question: What are the advantages of a Dual Special Needs plan?
atoms.text: Dual health plans offer benefits and services not typically available through Medicare or Medicaid alone. You keep your Medicaid benefits and get more benefits than Original Medicare, with as low as a $0 plan premium. UnitedHealthcare plans may cover routine dental care, a flexible monthly credit for healthy food, over-the-counter products and utility bills, eye exams plus credit for eyewear, and hearing exams plus credit for hearing devices. Some also include care coordination. Benefits vary by plan and area.

atoms.title: Three D-SNP eligibility questions
atoms.question: What are the eligibility requirements for Dual Special Needs plans?
atoms.text: 1) Do you get state Medicaid benefits? (You'd have a state Medicaid card.) 2) Do you have Medicare Parts A and B? You must be at least 65, or under 65 and qualify through disability or other special situations, and be a U.S. citizen or legal resident who has lived in the U.S. for at least 5 years in a row. 3) Do you live in an area where dual plans are available? A UnitedHealthcare licensed sales agent can tell you whether you live in the service area.

atoms.title: When can you apply for a D-SNP?
atoms.question: When can you apply for a Dual Special Needs Plan (D-SNP)?
atoms.text: Dual Special Needs plans have an ongoing Special Enrollment Period (SEP) that runs for the first 9 months of the year. People who qualify can enroll or change plans once every 3 months, and enrollment changes take effect the first day of the next month. To stay eligible you must recertify for Medicaid every year; as long as you stay eligible, your dual health plan will renew automatically each year.

atoms.title: How often can D-SNP members switch plans?
atoms.question: How often can members in Dual Special Needs plans switch plans?
atoms.text: D-SNP members can join, switch or drop their plan 1 time during each 3-month enrollment period: January to March, April to June, and July to September. A change takes effect on the first day of the next month. Members can also make changes during the Annual Enrollment Period from Oct. 15 to Dec. 7, with changes taking effect on Jan. 1 of the next year.

atoms.title: What happens if a D-SNP member loses Medicaid?
atoms.question: What happens when a D-SNP member loses Medicaid eligibility?
atoms.text: If you're enrolled in a UnitedHealthcare dual plan and lose Medicaid eligibility, UnitedHealthcare puts you on hold for 6 months. During that time you pay the Medicare cost-sharing portion, such as copayments, coinsurance, deductibles and premiums. If you don't regain Medicaid eligibility by the end of the 6 months, you'll be unenrolled from the dual plan. You can enroll in a dual plan at any time, so if you get Medicaid back, talk with a UnitedHealthcare licensed sales agent to re-enroll.

atoms.title: Is D-SNP enrollment state-based?
atoms.question: Is D-SNP enrollment by state?
atoms.text: Yes. Enrollment for Dual Special Needs plans is state-based. D-SNPs are offered in most states but not all, and the types of D-SNPs available and the benefits each provides can change depending on the county where you live. As of January 2025, UnitedHealthcare Community Plan serves members who qualify for Medicaid or for both Medicaid and Medicare in 43 states and the District of Columbia.

atoms.title: Standard D-SNP benefits, including dental and vision
atoms.question: What standard benefits are typically covered by UnitedHealthcare dual plans?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare dual plans typically cover preventive care and routine services at no extra cost, and offer help coordinating Medicaid benefits. Other standard benefits usually include dental, vision, hearing and transportation assistance. Dental coverage may include regular exams and cleanings plus an allowance toward fillings, root canals or implants. Vision coverage may include routine eye exams plus credits toward eyewear. Benefits vary by plan and service area.

atoms.title: How D-SNP costs are covered
atoms.question: Does Medicare cover D-SNP members' medical costs, and who pays the rest?
atoms.text: Since a D-SNP is a Medicare Advantage plan, Medicare covers most of the costs when members get medical care. The share that's left over, which may be called a premium, copay, coinsurance or deductible, is the member's responsibility, but for people on a D-SNP, state Medicaid programs help pay these costs. If you don't have Medicaid, your exact costs may depend on the plan you choose.

atoms.title: Coordination of benefits for D-SNPs
atoms.question: What is coordination of benefits?
atoms.text: Coordination of benefits (COB) applies to people with coverage under more than one health plan and determines which plan is the primary (first) payer and which is secondary. The primary payer coordinates delivery of all benefits and the secondary payer covers what the primary doesn't. A D-SNP is a Medicare Advantage plan that coordinates delivery of both Medicare and Medicaid benefits; in most cases Medicaid covers benefits and costs the D-SNP doesn't. D-SNPs also coordinate care management and disease management.

atoms.title: D-SNP vs. C-SNP vs. Medicare-Medicaid Plan
atoms.question: What is the difference between D-SNP, C-SNP and Medicare-Medicaid Plans (MMPs)?
atoms.text: A D-SNP is for low-income people dually eligible for Medicaid and Medicare. A C-SNP (Chronic Special Needs plan) is for people with a chronic condition such as chronic heart failure, cardiovascular disorders or diabetes. With a Medicare-Medicaid Plan (MMP), all Medicare and Medicaid benefits come through 1 single plan and only full dual eligibles can enroll. With a D-SNP, members keep their Medicaid plan and benefits plus a separate Medicare Advantage plan, and both full and partial dual eligibles can join.
questions: What is the difference between a D-SNP and a C-SNP?

atoms.title: D-SNPs are network-based; no referral needed in network
atoms.question: Are D-SNPs network-based, and do I need a referral to see a specialist?
atoms.text: Yes, D-SNPs are network-based, so members get care from doctors or hospitals in their plan's network. Networks vary in size and the populations they serve, for example a network may cover an entire state or a single county, or focus on a certain health issue such as dementia. When you have a UnitedHealthcare dual plan, referrals are not needed to get care from any in-network doctors, hospitals or clinics. Drug coverage is included, but check that your drugs are covered before you enroll.
